text: Thirty-seven war elephants. Over the Alps. In winter.
In two-hundred-eighteen BC, a Carthaginian general marched an army from Spain into Italy, the long way round, over the highest mountains in Europe.
Then he came within a whisker of destroying Rome.
So here is today's question. Why did Hannibal take the hardest road in the ancient world? And did it work?
Let's follow him on the map.
First, the grudge. Rome and Carthage were the two great powers of the western Mediterranean.
From two-hundred-sixty-four to two-hundred-forty-one BC they fought the First Punic War, mostly at sea. Rome won, and Carthage lost Sicily.
Carthage had to pay three-thousand-two-hundred talents of silver. Then Rome grabbed Sardinia and Corsica as well, and demanded more.
Even Polybius, a Greek historian who admired Rome, called the grab of Sardinia unjust.
A Carthaginian general, Hamilcar Barca, went west to Spain to build a new empire, rich in silver and soldiers.
His son-in-law founded a new capital on the Spanish coast: New Carthage. Today, it is Cartagena.
The story goes that he made his nine-year-old son swear never to be a friend of Rome. The boy's name was Hannibal.
In two-hundred-twenty-one BC, Hannibal took command in Spain. He was about twenty-six.
Two years later he besieged Saguntum, a Spanish city allied to Rome. It fell after eight months.
Rome declared war. The Second Punic War had begun.
Rome expected to fight in Spain and in Africa. After all, Rome now ruled the sea.
One Roman army headed for Spain. Another gathered in Sicily, ready to sail for Carthage itself.
Hannibal did the one thing nobody expected. He left the sea alone and went by land.
Polybius puts the route at about one-thousand-six-hundred kilometres. Through Spain, over the Pyrenees, across Gaul, and over the Alps.
Quick quiz. How long did the march from New Carthage to Italy take? Five weeks, five months, or a year?
Five months. About as long as Napoleon later spent getting to Moscow and back.
Polybius says he crossed the Ebro with ninety-thousand foot soldiers and twelve-thousand horsemen. Modern historians think that is too many.
And he brought thirty-seven war elephants.
North of the Ebro, the tribes fought him all the way. He left eleven-thousand men behind to hold the region, and sent about as many home.
By the time he crossed the Pyrenees, Polybius counts about fifty-thousand foot and nine-thousand horse.
In late September he reached the Rhône, a fast, wide river. On the far bank, a Gaulish tribe, the Volcae, was waiting.
Hannibal sent a force upstream under an officer named Hanno. They crossed at night on rafts, and came down behind the Gauls.
At a smoke signal, the main army crossed. Caught from both sides, the Gauls broke and ran.
Then the elephants. Hannibal's men built huge rafts and covered them with earth, so the animals thought they were still on land.
Some elephants panicked and fell into the river. Their drivers drowned, but the elephants swam across.
Meanwhile, a Roman army under the consul Scipio had landed at Massilia to stop him. It reached his camp three days too late.
Scipio made a bold call. He sent his army on to Spain under his brother, and hurried back to Italy himself.
Scipio could not believe it. Hannibal was not heading for Spain or the coast. He was heading for the Alps.
Polybius says about thirty-eight-thousand foot and eight-thousand horse left the Rhône. Ahead of them were the Alps, in autumn.
The passes he was heading for are well over two-thousand metres high. One of them is almost three-thousand.
Mountain tribes, the Allobroges, held the heights above the track, ready to roll rocks down on the column.
He even captured their town, and fed his army from its stores.
Hannibal waited for night, when the tribesmen went home to sleep, and quietly took the heights himself.
Still, the attacks came. In the narrow gorges, horses and pack animals fell off the cliffs with their loads.
The tribes were terrified of the elephants. Wherever the elephants walked, nobody attacked.
After nine days they reached the top. Snow had already fallen. It was late October, maybe early November.
The army rested there for two days. Men from Africa and Spain, who had never seen snow, stood freezing on the roof of Europe.
And the way down turned out to be worse than the way up.
On the Italian side, a landslide had swept the track away. There was no path left. Just a sheer slope of ice and rock.
The men dug a new track into the mountainside. The horses got through after one day.
The elephants waited three days, half-starved, before the road was wide enough.
Livy, writing two-hundred years later, says they cracked the rock with fire and vinegar. Polybius, the older source, never mentions it.
And which pass did they cross? Nobody knows. At least five passes have their supporters.
In twenty-sixteen, scientists found a layer of ancient horse dung below the Col de la Traversette, dated to around two-hundred BC. Interesting, but not proof.
But that date could be sixty years off, and no Carthaginian objects were found there. The mystery is still open.
A twenty-twenty-six study modelled how much energy each route would cost, and also picked the Traversette. Other historians are not convinced.
Quiz time. How many of the thirty-seven elephants made it over the Alps? None, about half, or most of them?
Most of them. Despite the legend, the elephants survived the Alps. It was what came next that killed them.
Hannibal reached the plains of northern Italy with twenty-thousand foot and six-thousand horse. We know, because he carved the numbers in bronze himself.
In fifteen days in the Alps, he had lost about half the army that left the Rhône. Many deserted. Many died.
Rome was stunned. In November, at the Ticinus river, Hannibal's cavalry routed the Romans. The consul Scipio was wounded.
In December, at the Trebia, he lured about forty-thousand Romans across an icy river and ambushed them. Only about ten-thousand broke out.
His brother Mago had hidden two-thousand men in a stream bed. When the Romans had crossed, they struck from behind.
But the winter that followed killed every elephant but one.
In the spring, Hannibal rode that last elephant through flooded marshes. He caught an infection there, and lost the sight of one eye.
In June two-hundred-seventeen BC, at Lake Trasimene, he hid his army in the hills. A Roman army marched along the shore, into the morning fog.
About fifteen-thousand Romans were killed in a few hours, including the consul Flaminius.
Rome panicked. It gave power to Fabius Maximus, who refused to fight a battle at all. He just followed Hannibal and wore him down.
Romans mocked him as the Delayer. By the next summer they wanted a real battle, and a big army to win it.
On the second of August two-hundred-sixteen BC, at Cannae, about eighty-six-thousand Romans faced Hannibal's fifty-thousand.
Hannibal put his weakest troops in the centre, bulging forward like a crescent, and his best African troops on the wings.
The Romans smashed into the centre. It slowly gave way, and pulled them in.
Then the African wings turned inward, and Hannibal's cavalry came round behind. The Romans were surrounded.
Polybius says about seventy-thousand Romans died that day. Livy says about forty-eight-thousand. Either way, it was one of the worst defeats in history.
One of the two consuls, Aemilius Paullus, died on the field. Rome had lost three armies in under two years.
Livy says one of Hannibal's officers told him: you know how to win a victory, Hannibal, but not how to use it.
So, did the hardest road work?
As a surprise, yes. The Alps let Hannibal skip Rome's navy and land an army in Italy that nobody was ready for.
But it came at a price. Half his army and almost all his elephants. And no siege engines to take Rome's walls.
Hannibal never besieged Rome. Rome refused to surrender, raised new armies, and kept him busy in Italy for fifteen years.
He had no siege engines, few reinforcements from home, and most of Rome's allies in central Italy stayed loyal.
In two-hundred-three BC Carthage called him home. A year later, at Zama, a Roman general named Scipio, the son of the consul at the Rhône, beat him.
Years later, in exile and about to be handed over to Rome, Hannibal took poison.
Rome won the war. But generals still study Cannae today, and the road over the Alps is still the most famous march in history.
Now, your turn. After Cannae, should Hannibal have marched straight on Rome? Tell me in the comments.
